chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
title: Hired as arranger: the band's few arrangements and Trumbauer's book
summary: Horvath said saxophonists were plentiful but arrangers were not; Trumbauer's St. Louis arrangements and Don Murray's work are discussed, with Jack Pettis.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Were you playing with the band?

No. Well, when he called me into to talk to me, he said -- I asked him, if he wanted me to play -- Do you want Horvath, the manager, if he wanted me to play. What did he want me to do with my horns? "Don't worry about it," but he says, "I'll tell you, why don't you do this. Saxophone players are a dime a dozen. I can get them. I can't get any arrangers." And he said, "We only have seven arrangements." Well, seven arrangements, I guess what he meant by that was of the top tunes of the day, because they played all kinds of things. They played Singing the Blues, they played all those cuties that Trumbauer and Bix -- Trumbauer had a band previously to this in St. Louis and he had PeeWee Russell and he had Bix and he had several other guys there too -- I can't remember their names offhand, but I guess it was a pretty good band, and they worked out a lot of things and of course, when he joined the Goldkette band, he brought

those things along and a lot of them were memorized and a lot of them were put down like -- the Bix part would be written up, Trumbauer's part would be written up and then maybe some other part that they needed. The rhythm wouldn't be in there at all, so they had several of those things that they brought up and they played all -- a lot of Dixieland things that they later made records of with Trumbauer and with Bix, not with Goldkette.

The Goldkette band was a different thing. The only thing that they had and that they had set up was My Pretty Girl which is a fantastic thing anyway, and it had three trumpet, you know, Trumbauer played a great part in that, and the ensemble was good. They also had an arrangement of the --that Don Murray had made. The name doesn't come right now. But it was a fine arrangement. He was an excellent musician. Good arranger. But you couldn't get him to do anything, like a lot of guys.

I remember seeing a picture of him and he seemed like a very handsome guy, too, in fact, at the time that I saw the picture, you know, maybe 15 years ago or so, I drew a parallel with Stan Getz. He reminded me of Getz in this picture. I don't know what he looked like in real life.
I remember at the time -- what's that early tenor saxophone player Jack -- that used to play around New York.
He used to talk a lot about Jack Pettis.
Bud Freeman did too to me a lot.
Yeah, he mentioned Jack Pettis. He liked Jack Pettis.
